chapters.name: 2. FARMSTEAD
chapters.label: 2. FARMSTEAD

subchapters.name: CHAPTER 2 BUILDINGS AND ROADS
subchapters.label: Buildings and Roads
subchapters.description:
On most farms, the yard, buildings and access roads are the heart of day‑to‑day work. How you place, build and maintain them can protect water, soil, air and habitat—and also reduce complaints from neighbours. Roofs, paved yards and roads change how rain runs off your land, which can lead to erosion or flooding if not managed well. Stream crossings and work near ditches or creeks can affect fish and wildlife. This section explains these risks in plain terms and shows you how to manage them.

 

Planning ahead pays off. This chapter points to the rules that may apply to your farm and reminds you to factor in climate risks like wildfire and heavy rain that can raise flood risk. Smart siting, drainage, and construction choices can lower those risks and protect your operation for the long term.

 

If you’re completing an Environmental Farm Plan, use this section alongside support from an EFP Planning Advisor. Walk your yard after a storm to see where water flows, note any crossings, and check whether building locations and roads are working with—not against—your land and neighbours.

subchapters.name: CHAPTER 2 CHEMICAL FERTILIZER
subchapters.label: Chemical Fertilizer
subchapters.description:
Fertilizers help crops grow, but if they’re not handled properly, they can harm water, soil, and air. Extra nutrients can wash into streams and lakes, causing algae blooms and fish kills. Spills or poor storage can also contaminate drinking water. Some fertilizers, like ammonium nitrate, are even a fire risk if stored near fuel or heat sources.

 

This section explains how to store, handle, and apply fertilizers safely. You’ll learn about the rules that apply in B.C. and practical steps to reduce risk—like keeping fertilizers away from wells and ditches, using proper containment, and applying the right amount at the right time.

Good fertilizer management saves money and protects your land. It also helps you meet environmental standards and avoid complaints from neighbors. If you’re working on your Environmental Farm Plan, use this section with your Planning Advisor to check your current practices and plan improvements.

 

The goal is simple: keep nutrients where your crops need them and out of places they don’t belong.

subchapters.name: CHAPTER 2 FARM WASTE
subchapters.label: FARM WASTE
subchapters.description:
Every farm produces waste—old fencing, plastic, used oil, animal health products, and more. If these materials aren’t managed properly, they can pollute soil and water, harm wildlife, and create safety hazards. Burning or dumping waste in the wrong place can also break the law and damage your reputation.

 

This section covers the main types of farm waste and how to deal with them responsibly. You’ll find tips on reducing waste, reusing materials, and recycling where possible. For items that can’t be reused, we explain safe disposal options, including permitted landfills and take-back programs for things like paint and pesticides.

 

Managing waste well isn’t just about compliance—it’s about protecting your farm and community. It reduces fire risk, keeps harmful chemicals out of the environment, and shows customers you care about sustainability.

 

If you’re completing an Environmental Farm Plan, walk through this section with your Planning Advisor. Together, you can identify problem areas and set up a plan that works for your operation.

questions.label: 161. Are mortalities handled in a way that protects water, air, and nearby properties, and keeps animals and pests away?
questions.textAboveQuestion: The Code of Practice for Agricultural Environmental Management makes provisions for on-farm mortality disposal through composting, burial and incineration provided that the disposal activities are carried out on the farm  where the animal died.
questions.textBelowQuestion:
Follow these practices to safely handle mortalities and stay within AEM Code regulations:

  • Mortalities disposed of on the farm are from your farm.
  • Mortalities are kept out of watercourses.
  • Runoff, leachate, solids, and air emissions from mortality disposal do not enter surface water, groundwater, or cross property boundaries.
  • Odours and particles are controlled, and the site does not attract pets, wildlife, or pests.
  • Mortalities are stored in a way that prevents rotting and leaking.

questions.label: 167. Are mortalities disposed of using the most preferred method?
questions.textBelowQuestion: Refer to Table 3.5 for preferred methods of mortality disposal based on cause of death.

questions.label: 168. Are mortality composting sites the required distance away from water sources and property boundaries?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
• 30 m (100 ft) from a drinking water source or watercourse
  • 15 m (50 ft) from a watercourse if composting is done in a structure
  • 4.5 m (13.5 ft) from a property boundary

questions.label: 169. Is mortality composting done in a way that protects water, air, and soil, and follows composting best practices?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
When composting mortalities, you must meet these conditions:

  • Composting is done in a structure or outdoor pile that prevents runoff, leachate, and solids from escaping.
  • Air emissions from composting do not cross property boundaries.
  • Mortalities are fully decomposed before land application, and if exporting poultry mortality compost, it is mixed with poultry manure at barn clean-out (max 10% of total volume).
  • Outdoor composting piles are placed away from standing water, saturated soil, or flood-prone areas.
  • Outdoor composting piles are moved within 15 months.
  • The same composting location is not used more than once every 3 years.

questions.label: 175. If you compost specified risk material (SRM), do you only apply it to land that isn’t used for food crops or grazing animals?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
“Specified risk material” means parts of a cow that could carry disease, including:

  • Brain, spinal cord, and related tissues from cattle 30 months or older.
  • A section of the gut (distal ileum) from any cattle.

chapters.name: 6. NUTRIENT APPLICATION
chapters.label: 6. NUTRIENT APPLICATION
chapters.description:
Applying nutrients to your farm—like manure, compost, or fertilizer—is essential for growing healthy crops. But how and when you apply them matters. 

 

One key approach is the “4R” method: using the Right Source, at the Right Rate, at the Right Time, and in the Right Place. This helps you match nutrients to your crop’s needs while reducing waste and environmental risks. 

 

Check out BC's EFP Reference Guide Chapter 6 for practical tips for managing manure, choosing soil amendments, and planning nutrient applications throughout the year. 

 

Whether you’re growing forage, berries, vegetables, or tree fruit, this chapter helps you make informed decisions that benefit your farm and the land around it.

subchapters.name: Introduction: Nutrient Application
subchapters.label: INTRODUCTION
subchapters.description:
Nutrient Sources and the Environment: what you need to know
 

Why nutrients matter
Plants need nutrients to grow. Those nutrients come from fertilizers, manure, soil amendments, and nitrogen fixed by legumes. Each source behaves differently in soil and water—and each can create risk if over‑applied or poorly managed.

 

Understand the basics
This section explains how nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium work, and why soil pH and salts matter. It also covers secondary nutrients, micronutrients, and metals, plus the difference between nutrient sources and soil conditioners.

 

Watch for problem areas
Learn how to avoid phosphorus build‑up, check amendments for contaminants, and choose the right material for your fields.

 

Plan with confidence
Pair this section with tools like the Nutrient Management Calculator and your EFP Planning Advisor to keep nutrients where crops need them and out of waterways.

 

Nutrient Application: the 4R basics
 

Start with the 4Rs
Right Source, Right Rate, Right Time, Right Place—this section shows how to apply these principles on your farm.

 

Match source to crop and soil
Choose the right product for your crop and conditions.

 

Set a rate you can defend
Use soil tests and realistic yield goals to avoid over‑application.

 

Time it to crop demand
Apply nutrients when plants can use them. Split applications may help for long‑season crops.

 

Place to protect water
Position nutrients so crops get them and waterways don’t.

 

Check your work
Calibrate spreaders and sprayers, and use post‑harvest nitrate tests to see if your plan worked.

 

Know the rules
This section also summarizes B.C. regulations and setbacks for nutrient application.

questions.label: 259. Is nutrient application managed to ensure that nutrient sources do not move off site, enter environmentally sensitive areas, and follow legislated setbacks?
questions.textBelowQuestion:
You must meet these conditions:

  • Use a risk assessment tool, such as the BC ARM Tool, to determine the risk of nutrient loss in runoff within 24 hours of application
  • Avoid application during poor conditions, such as heavy precipitation, strong winds, or water tables near the soil surface
  • Avoid application during periods where crops do not take up nutrients (including having enough storage capacity for manure to store all manure during this period)
  • Observe setbacks and adjust them based on current field conditions, slope, and soil drainage capacity
  • Use vegetative buffers to reduce the risk of nutrient loss in runoff
  • Adjust application to avoid discharge directly into tile drains
